messages.subject: Missing data
parts:
Hello team,

I am working with some data that has a lot of missing values, because of the way sites were sampled. Not every site was surveyed every year, and when a site was surveyed, the number of visits within a year varies. I think I've gotten the indexing correct to deal with the structure of the data, but I was curious about how nimble was treating those missing values. I assumed they would be ignored, but when I monitored the data, it looks like those missing values are being estimated (at least they go from NA to some non NA value). Curious why that might be? In JAGS, when I've done this, those site x year x occasion values have remained missing if I were to monitor the data. 

Any insight would be appreciated. Thanks again for creating nimble! Its making it much more efficient to run some of these CAR models!

Cheers,
Paige

messages.author: 442b578d148ed4d1
messages.subject: Re: Missing data
parts:
Hi Paige,

I'm not connected with the nimble team, but I believe that this is a general Bayesian/MCMC question so I'm going to jump in (and hope that I don't stick my foot in my mouth).

In Bayesian inference you can define the posterior distribution for any collection of random variables (i.e., unknown quantities). A common way to handle missing data in Bayesian inference is to treat missing data in exactly the same way as the observed data by defining the joint pmf/pdf as if these values had been observed. The resulting likelihood function is often referred to as the complete data likelihood since it defines the likelihood (the pmf/pdf as a function of the parameters not the data) as if you had the complete data set in hand.

Using this likelihood you can then construct the posterior distribution for the parameters alone by summing/integrating across the values of the missing data or you can construct the posterior distribution of all the unknown variables, including both the parameters and the the missing data value.

MCMC is simply a method to sample from the posterior distribution defined by the model. If you have missing data for which the pmf/pdf has been defined then samplers will include this variables as part of the posterior distribution and provide samples. You can interpret the distribution formed from these samples as providing information about what the true value would have been if you had observed it. E.g., the posterior median for a missing data values indicates that you believe the truth has a 50-50 chance of being above or below that value. 

Without knowing more about your model and your JAGS/nimble code I am more surprised that JAGS didn't provide samples for these values than that nimble did. 

I hope that's helpful.

Cheers,

Simon

messages.author: e523634175c37160
messages.subject: Re: Missing data
parts:
Thanks for your thoughtful response Simon. 

I probably should have provided an example in my first post, my apologies! Below is a snippet of code related to my initial question. The part highlighted in red is my data (counts at each site, each year, on each sampling occasion). The indexing is intended to skip over site x year x occasion combinations where there was no survey, since there is no data there to contribute to the likelihood. I expected that those observations would remain missing, but when I monitor the data, it does seem like they are being updated from NA to some non NA value. 

  for(t in 1:nYears){ # 2010-2019
    # Derived parameter - total abundance each year, across study area
    Ntot[t] <- sum(N[1:nSites,t]) 
   
    # likelihood
    for(i in 1:nSites){ # loop over grid cells 
      # Realized abundance each year and grid cell
      N[i,t] ~ dpois(lambda[i,t])
     
      # Expected abundance each year and grid cell.
      # Varies as a function of covariate and includes a spatial random effect
      log(lambda[i,t]) <- alpha1*cov[i,t] + rho[i] 

    # CAR prior distribution for spatial random effects - 1st order CAR
    rho[1:nSites] ~ dcar_normal(adj[1:L], weights[1:L], num[1:nSites], tauSp, zero_mean=0)
     }
   
    for(i in 1:nSitesSampled[t]){ # Grid cells surveyed each year
      for(j in 1:nReps[t,i]){ # Number of reps (1 or 2) within each grid cell, each year
        # Count data: Number of birds observed in each grid cell, each year, on each survey
        C[site[t,i],t,j] ~ dbin(p[site[t,i],t,j], N[site[t,i],t])
        Cnew[site[t,i],t,j] ~ dbin(p[site[t,i],t,j], N[site[t,i],t]) # replicate data set
       
        # Detection probability
        # Intercept varies by vehicle: airplane is the intercept, effect of helicopter is kappa1, and amount of a grid cell covered by each survey (effort)
        logit(p[site[t,i],t,j]) <- kappa0 + kappa1*vehicle[site[t,i],t,j] + kappa2*effort[site[t,i],t,j]
        }}}

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Missing data
parts:
Paige, thanks for the question.  Simon, thanks for jumping in.

By coincidence multiple nimble core developers have limited availability this week.

If I follow, your indexing scheme makes sense.  I don't totally follow C vs Cnew.  I'm not sure whether you want both or whether one is a temporary piece of code.  If one of them (Cnew?) is intended for posterior prediction, it would be more efficient if you are able to do that as a separate step, after the MCMC.  I realize that can present logistical hurdles of monitoring what is needed, but the monitors2 and thin2 system may be helpful.  You can use a nimble model for simulation, so you can for example iterate through a sample, use values() <- or nimCopy to put values into a model, and use model$simulate to simulate new values.  This can be done from R for a compiled model or in a nimbleFunction that you can also compile. But anyway that wasn't your question.

On to your question: we will have to look more carefully later to investigate your report of different behavior of JAGS and NIMBLE for NAs interspersed arbitrarily among C[site index, time index, rep index] values.  In the meantime, here are two suggested workarounds.  The first, which will be easier if it works, will be simply to provide non-NA values in those elements of C that are not data.  The only reason to provide NA is to indicate that you want them sampled.  If you provide non-NA values for elements that are not in a declared node (i.e. not declared in the model code), they will (or should) simply be unused.  You could verify that by providing values like -1 that would generate an error if for some reason they are being used when they shouldn't be.  In summary, try replacing your NAs with -1.

The second solution would be to remove samplers from the sampler configuration for the missing data nodes. To do this, you would need to explicitly create your MCMC configuration (as opposed to using nimbleMCMC, for example).  Then you would do something like

Rmodel <- nimbleModel( <your arguments> ) ## with NAs in C to indicate which elements are not data
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
# mcmcConf$printSamplers("C") ## do this to see what samplers were assigned, if any, to elements of C and confirm they are for the NA elements
mcmcConf$removeSamplers("C")
# mcmcConf$printSamplers("C") ## do this to verify the result of the previous line

Note that there shouldn't be samplers for data elements of C, so the only samplers would be for non-data elements of C, which are the one you don't want.  If it was more complicated, I would think of tools like Rmodel$isData and Rmodel$expandNodeNames to put together which elements of C are relevant.

Please let us know if one of these ideas works.

-Perry
